Problem solved. In the current case, the above error results from (a) the class of object referenced in the LHS of the formula passed to the function "summary;" and (b) my confusion regarding the expected class of object returned from a call to networkDynamic::network.extract. The R help file for network.extract suggests that a networkDynamic _or_ network object will be returned depending on the setting of the "retain.all.vertices" argument. Further, the tutorial at https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Resources/STERGMtutorial.pdf shows the successful use of network.extract to obtain a cross-section for evaluation. What was not clear to me was that the tutorial dataset was not a networkDynamic object. A simple example should suffice as evidence of problem and resolution:

___BEGIN SNIPPET___
> class(flobusiness)  # tutorial dataset for which stergm does not throw an error.
[1] "network"
> class(dyn)  # my dataset.
[1] "networkDynamic" "network"

> x1 <- network.extract(dyn, at=2006)
> class(x1)
[1] "networkDynamic" "network"
> summary(x1~edges)
Error in lapply(X = X, FUN = FUN, ...) :
  argument "at" is missing, with no default

> x2 <- network.extract(dyn, at=2006, retain.all.vertices=TRUE)
> class(x2)
[1] "networkDynamic" "network"
> summary(x2~edges)
Error in lapply(X = X, FUN = FUN, ...) :
  argument "at" is missing, with no default

> flat <- network.collapse(dyn, at=2006)
> class(flat)
[1] "network"
> summary(flat~edges)
edges
    2
___END SNIPPET___

So, I'll simply use network.collapse going forward. :)

Respectfully,
Brent Fegley
doctoral student, Informatics
University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet developers and community,

I published an ERGM analysis in the American Journal of Political 
Science last year:

Leifeld, Philip and Volker Schneider (2012): Information Exchange in 
Policy Networks. American Journal of Political Science 53(3): 731-744. 
http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2011.00580.x

Replication data and code: http://hdl.handle.net/1902.1/17004

I was using the following package versions:

sna 2.1-0 (2010-04-15)
network 1.6 (2011-01-28)
ergm 2.4 (2011-05-24)

I am now trying to replicate my own results using the current versions 
of these packages:

sna 2.3-1 (2013-02-28)
network 1.7.2 (2013-03-15)
ergm 3.1-0 (2013-04-17)

However, although I am using exactly the same code and data including 
the same random seed in the ergm command, the results are very different.

The estimation in the new version takes much longer and shows signs of 
degeneracy (20 iterations between which the log-likelihood increases by 
more than 10, sometimes almost 20, each time). The diagnostics look 
quite OK though.

I installed the old package versions on another machine and there I can 
in fact replicate my old results. So why am I having degeneracy problems 
in the new version despite using the same data, commands, seed etc.? I 
have tried to increase the MCMC sample size to 50k, and I set 
MCMC.interval = 1000, but this does not help.

Any help would be appreciated. Thanks!

Philip

influenced by other dependencies and changes in the code -- it's 
unfortunate but unavoidable.  But the appearance of degeneracy is a 
different issue.  I think that suggests that the model was probably close 
to degenerate in the original case as well.

Thanks for your reply. Meanwhile I replicated the estimation four times 
using the old package and four times using the new package, each time 
without any explicit random seed. All of the four estimation runs based 
on the OLD package yield very similar estimates and SEs (not identical, 
but very similar), are computed fairly fast, do not show any signs of 
degeneracy, show a good model fit, and look plausible. All of the four 
estimation runs based on the NEW package version yield estimates and SEs 
which are very different both from the four previous models and from 
each other; they also take longer to compute, and they show fairly large 
changes in the log likelihood between all iterations. So this does not 
seem to depend on the seed, and it also looks like the model was not 
close to degenerate in the original case. I may be wrong, but to me this 
looks like the new, rather than the old, models are degenerate.

Philip

Hi, Philip -

As others have noted, there has been a lot of development (particularly 
in the estimation procedures) since early 2011, so it's challenging to 
pin down the exact source of the changes you are seeing.  If you have 
both versions running, one thing that would be helpful would be to 
verify that you are getting the same statistics for your observed 
network in both versions.  In general, if you have an ergm formula of 
the form mynet~myterms, you can get the observed statistics via

summary(mynet~myterms)

I don't think any of the publicly available statistics have changed 
(though others should correct me if I am wrong), so you should get the 
same results on the old and new code.  If not, it's certainly worth 
mentioning, because that could explain the changes in your results.  
(And such a change might indicate a bug, so we'd like to be aware of 
it!)  If you find that your observed stats haven't changed between 
versions, that at least eliminates one possible source for the discrepancy.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, David.  Missing data on attributes makes certain kinds of 
changescores indeterminate; there are ways to deal with that, but IIRC 
they're not currently built into ergm.  (The main exceptions are some 
categorical terms that by default treat NA as if it were a distinct 
category.)  I was actually under the impression that ergm _always_ 
produced an error when the changescore was poorly defined, so if you 
were able to fit those models before, that might have been due to a bug 
that was fixed.  :-)

Mark and Ian have been thinking about this problem more than I have, and 
so may have a grander suggestion than my pragmatic one. My short-term 
suggestion would be to estimate your model via a two-stage procedure: 
first, impute your missing attribute data using a standard imputation 
method; and second, fit the ergm given the imputed data.  (It would 
probably be wise to create multiple imputed data sets in this manner, 
and examine the distribution of estimates across imputed values.)  This 
is not 100% ideal, but will probably work well so long as the results 
are not very sensitive to the missing values.  If the results _are_ 
sensitive to the missing values (something you can determine by looking 
at the distribution of estimates across imputed data sets), then you are 
likely in a bad spot regardless, and no method is going to be entirely 
trustworthy.  (See also, "you can only get a loan when you don't need it.")

By contrast, if you have missing data in the edges, ergm will indeed 
handle that.  (Or, at least, it will try.  You may still lack the power 
needed to answer your question of interest!)  The approach employed is 
the latent missing data technique developed by Gile and Handcock.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM error
messages.body_plain:
Hello Ngoni,

My guess is that you attached the igraph package to your session after 
you attached statnet.  Unfortunately, when igraph was developed in 2006, 
the author used some function names that were already in use in the 
network package (the latter on CRAN at the time as an independent 
package, and then subsequently part of the statnet suite).  That means 
that now, if one attaches both, then whichever one gets attached later 
will be the source of the functions drawn when they are shared. If 
you're trying to use statnet functionality, this can cause problems, as 
it is expecting the network functionality, but if you attach igraph 
later it uses igraph functionality.

One piece of evidence that suggests this is that it says

Error in is.directed(x) : Not a graph object

package 'network' uses 'network' objects, and package 'igraph' uses 
'graph' objects.

If you're trying to use statnet functionality (e.g. ergm), I'd recommend 
either sticking with network for your data management, or, if you do 
want some of the additional igraph functionality, to make sure to attach 
igraph before statnet, so that it won't override some of the network 
functions.

Hope that helps,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Ngoni and others,

Two points:

First, Steve is very much correct that the error you are getting is
because you have loaded and attached network package first and then
igraph. To dodge the problem you have to detach igraph package before
running ergm by calling 'detach(package:igraph)'. If you are
interested in more details see my blog post here:
http://bc.bojanorama.pl/2010/08/namespaces-and-name-conflicts/

Second point is more of a suggestion to statnet developers. The
problem is indirectly caused by the fact that package 'ergm' specifies
the 'network' package as a dependency through the "Depends" field in
its DESCRIPTION file. This mechanism is very fragile to the presence
of other packages the user may have loaded and attached (like 'igraph'
in Ngoni's case). The preferred mechanism would be for 'ergm' to
import 'network' package (just like 'network' package imports 'utils'
package). Without going into even more technical details (which are
available upon request :) ), the difference is that 'ergm's internal
code will be guaranteed to always try to use 'network's functions
first, and only later look in the global environment (workspace).

You can try it yourself by modifying the source of 'ergm' by
1. Modifying DESCRIPTION by moving 'network' from "Depends:" to "Imports:"
2. Adding 'import(network)' to NAMESPACE file.

The only side effect would be that if you load 'ergm' by using
'library(ergm)' the network package will be loaded, but *not*
attached. The user would have to do that himself. If auto-attaching
'network' when attaching 'ergm' is so desired, that could be done by
adding the '.onAttach' hook to 'ergm' that would also load and attach
'network'.

Best,
Michal

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michal,

I would argue that in this case ergm is doing the right thing to depend on network not just import. The Depends field is reserved for dependancies which, if not loaded by the user, renders the package virtually unusable. This is the case with the network package as it provides the fundamental data structure upon which all ergm functions operate. ergm does have a number of pacakges which should be imported rather than depended upon. The trust package are the most obvious of these as the user will never call trust directly.

That said, ergm should probably also import network to prevent internal functions from calling into igraph. This way the user can have both loaded, and distinguish between the two with network::is.directed and igraph::is.directed in their own code.


Ian
